standard.title: Communicate ideas and arguments
standard.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments for specific purposes and audiences, including selection of appropriate language and text features, using digital tools as appropriate
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can write and create texts to communicate ideas and findings for specific purposes and audiences (AC9S5I06). They have not yet selected language and text features strategically for purpose and audience or produced multi-modal scientific communications.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments for specific purposes and audiences, selecting appropriate language and text features and using digital tools as appropriate.

nodes.label: Purpose, audience and text type
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose and audience of scientific texts and select an appropriate text type
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the purpose and target audience of a given scientific text; explain how the text type suits the audience
nodes.typical_width: Examine a range of scientific texts; infer purpose and audience from language and text features; select appropriate text types for different communication purposes
wider: Compare how the same scientific finding is communicated in a journal article, a news report and a social media post — explain what changes and why
Evaluate a scientific text that is poorly matched to its audience and explain what should change
Analyse how First Nations Australians scientists communicate science to diverse audiences and what text features they use

response_modes.reason: Students commonly write for a generic audience rather than making deliberate choices about language, detail level and text features for a specific reader. Examining multiple text types across different purposes — journal, news, social media, letter to editor, animation — helps students see that communication is a design decision, not a fixed format. Each new text type reveals different choices and trade-offs.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations scientists communication direction — analysing how communicators like Kirsten Banks bridge Indigenous and Western scientific knowledge for diverse audiences — is rich beyond the minimum. It connects to AC9S7H02 and H04, and gives advancing students a case where communication purpose and audience are genuinely complex and the text features are purposefully chosen.
success_criteria: Identifies the purpose and target audience of a scientific text
Explains how the text type suits the audience
Does not assume all scientific communication uses the same format

nodes.label: Language and text features for science communication
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and use appropriate language and text features including diagrams, graphical representations and data
nodes.minimum_width: Report on a scientific investigation using at least one diagram or graphical representation; communicate findings to a known audience
nodes.typical_width: Produce a scientific report incorporating diagrams, graphical representations and data; examine accuracy and reproducibility of data; select language features appropriate to purpose
wider: Create an informative text for a younger audience explaining a science concept (e.g. seasons, particle theory) — adapt language and representations appropriately
Write a letter to the editor expressing a science-informed view about a local environmental issue
Create an animation explaining a science concept to a peer audience using digital tools

response_modes.reason: Incorporating diagrams, data and scientific language into written reports is a precision skill. Students commonly include representations without integrating them into the text — diagrams are decorative, not referenced in the writing. Practice producing reports where text and representations are explicitly connected is what helps, not more communication contexts.

success_criteria: Includes at least one diagram or graphical representation
Representation is referenced in the text, not just appended
Language is appropriate for the stated audience

nodes.label: Communicating for specific purposes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write and create texts that communicate ideas, findings and arguments effectively for a specific purpose and audience
nodes.minimum_width: Produce a scientific communication for a specific purpose and audience; select text type and language features appropriate to that purpose
nodes.typical_width: Produce communications for two different purposes or audiences; explain and justify the choices made about text type, language and representations in each
wider: Develop a prototype dichotomous key app to enable community members to classify organisms in a local park or reserve
Create a multi-modal scientific communication (e.g. video, poster, interactive tool) and evaluate its effectiveness for the target audience
Produce a scientific communication that integrates findings from multiple investigations into a coherent argument

response_modes.reason: This node integrates purpose/audience awareness (Node 1), language and representation skills (Node 2), and argument construction from AC9S7I07 into a coordinated communication product. Students who can address each element separately but cannot produce a text that coordinates all three have not met the descriptor's full communicative demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The dichotomous key app direction is rich — it requires students to translate classification knowledge (AC9S7U01), representation skills (AC9S7I04), and communication design into an interactive digital tool for a community audience. This goes well beyond the minimum communication task and connects multiple strands into genuine applied work.
success_criteria: Produces a communication for a specific purpose and audience
Text type and language features are appropriate to the purpose
Communication includes ideas, findings or arguments — not just description
